hints: Notice where X and Y sit on the rope relative to the crossing points where the solid and dashed lines meet.
Recall how all particles between two adjacent nodes of a stationary wave move - they pass through zero and reach the extremes at the same instant.
Check whether X and Y ever move in opposite directions in the solid and dashed extreme positions shown.
walkthrough: Identify the stationary-wave pattern: the crossing points of the solid and dashed lines are the nodes where displacement is always zero.
Locate X and Y: both are marked inside the same central loop, bounded on the left and right by the same pair of adjacent nodes.
State the rule for a stationary wave: all particles between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase with each other, while particles in neighbouring loops oscillate in antiphase.
Apply the rule: in the solid-line instant X and Y are both above the centre, and in the dashed-line instant both are below the centre, so they reach maximum, zero and minimum together.
Therefore the phase difference between X and Y is $0$, with no lead or lag. This is option A

options.A: X and Y lie in the same loop between the same two nodes, so they move up and down together in phase.
options.B: A $45^{\circ}$ shift would mean X and Y reach maximum at different times, which does not happen inside one stationary-wave loop.
options.C: A $90^{\circ}$ shift applies to different relationships such as displacement versus velocity, not to two points in the same loop.
options.D: A large shift such as $135^{\circ}$ would require X and Y to be in different loops or on opposite sides of a node.
